power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Questionable research practices in music psychology: self-reported use and perceived prevalence
table.research_questions:
RQ1. Does self-reported Questionable Research Practice (QRP) engagement differ across career stage?

RQ2. Is mean perceived prevalence higher than the sample's own admission rate for the same practice?

RQ3. What proportion of respondents admit each of the 22 practices at least once, with particular attention to the five music-specific items, for which no prior estimate exists in any field?

RQ4. Is a higher count of open research practices associated with a lower QRP admission rate?

H1. Perceived prevalence of questionable research practices among music psychology researchers positively predicts a respondent's own self-reported QRP engagement.

H1a. Within a respondent, the practices they rate as more prevalent in the field are the practices they are likelier to admit.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data exists but the authors have not observed it yet. At least some of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists and is possible for the authors to access. However, the authors certify that they have not accessed any of that data and will not do so until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Non-randomized study: Does not include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes correlational studies, observational studies, surveys, natural experiments, real-world evidence studies, regression discontinuity designs, and descriptive studies.
table.intention_for_causal_interpretation: Indirect inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to examine a potential causal relationship, but is not designed to isolate the specific causal effect. This work may inform causal inference indirectly or advance insight toward future estimation of a causal relationship.
table.study_design_overview:
Cross-sectional anonymous online survey, no experimental manipulation and no randomisation of item order.

Self-report precedes prevalence estimation for every respondent. This ordering is fixed and is not counterbalanced. It follows the source surveys (see next paragraph) and protects the self-admissions from being anchored on a respondent's own estimate of the field. This also leaves a carryover path in the other direction: a respondent who has just admitted a practice may raise their estimate of how common it is. As H1 regresses admission on estimate, that carryover is a live alternative explanation and is named as a limitation.

The instrument follows the self-admission plus prevalence-estimate design of John, Loewenstein and Prelec (2012), and adapted for a non-psychology field by Fraser and colleagues (2018), who likewise asked researchers to estimate the proportion of colleagues using each practice. Changes from those studies: a frequency scale instead of a binary admission, and five items written for music psychology specifically (musical stimulus swapping, definitions of musical training, musically based inclusion criteria, audio and MIR feature selection, preprocessing pipelines for physiological, motion and neural data). Those five items have no prior benchmark in any field and are the novel contribution of the descriptive results.
table.data_collection_procedures:
The target population is researchers who have authored at least one empirical output in music psychology or a closely related field (music perception, music cognition, music therapy research, performance science, music education research, systematic musicology, music information retrieval) in the past five to seven years. Data are collected via a single anonymous online survey (Webropol), open to anyone reached through the recruitment channels.

Recruitment includes direct email to authors of recent music psychology publications, mailing lists of relevant societies such as ESCOM, and through social media.

Eligibility is screened within the survey itself: respondents must consent (Q1) and confirm empirical authorship in the field within the past five to seven years (Q2); those who fail either are not analysed. No further exclusions are applied prior to analysis.
table.sample_size: Single-level design at the respondent level. there are no conditions, treatments or clusters to compare, since this is a non-randomised survey. Target N is 100–150 eligible, consenting respondents who complete at least the self-report block (Q4–Q7). The design does have a nested structure within-person: each respondent answers up to 22 practice items twice (self-reported use, then perceived prevalence), so the item-level analysis treats items (level 1, up to 22 observations) as nested within respondents (level 2, 100–150 respondents).
table.sample_size_rationale: The target of 100–150 respondents was set as a feasibility-based constraint, informed by a directly comparable survey in this literature: a 2025 survey of music psychology authors on data-sharing practices, using similar recruitment channels, achieved 149 completed responses from 1,553 deliverable invitations (a 9.6% response rate; Eerola, 2026, in revision). This range was checked against a sensitivity analysis for the primary hypothesis test: at N = 100–150, the design can detect a correlation of r ≈ .23–.28 at 80% power (α = .05, two-tailed), meaning it is adequately powered for a moderate association.
table.stopping_rule: Following the timeline used in a directly comparable survey in this literature (Eerola, 2026, in revision, which collected data over a three-month window with a one-month reminder to non-respondents), data collection will remain open for three months from launch (closes November, 2026), with a single reminder sent to non-respondents approximately one month in, where the recruitment channel permits this (e.g., direct email; not applicable to open links or forwarded invitations). The closing date is fixed at launch.
table.manipulated_variables: None. This is a non-randomised survey with no experimental manipulation and no random assignment to conditions.
table.measured_variables:
Primary predictor and outcome (H1). For each of 22 research practices, respondents report (a) their own frequency of use in the past five to seven years (Never / Once / 2–3 times / More than 3 times / Not applicable to my research / Prefer not to answer) and (b) their estimate of the percentage of music psychology researchers who have used it at least once (0–10% / 11–25% / 26–50% / 51–75% / 76–100% / No opinion). The 22 items span four content areas: generic reporting and data-collection practices (6 items), generic analysis and reporting practices (7 items), music-specific practices such as stimulus selection and musical-training definitions (5 items), and publication/citation conduct (4 items).

Additional measured variables. Open research practices used (5 items: preregistration, data sharing, code/materials sharing, replication attempts, preprints; Never/Once/2–3 times/More than 3 times/Prefer not to answer). Publication pressure and perceived detectability (4 items, 5-point agreement scale). Eligibility/screening: empirical authorship in the field (yes/no) and extent of quantitative work (3-level).

Covariates and subsetting variables. Career stage (7-level categorical), years since PhD (6-level ordinal), region (7-level categorical), gender (4-level categorical), primary research area (9-level categorical), number of peer-reviewed articles authored (5-level ordinal), typical sample size in led studies (7-level ordinal). These are used as covariates in secondary models (RQ1, RQ4) and as the basis for planned exclusions and sensitivity subsets (e.g., restricting to quantitative researchers, excluding "Other" research area).
table.indices:
QRP admission rate (primary outcome for H1): number of the 22 practice items admitted (coded 1 if response is Once/2–3 times/More than 3 times, 0 if Never) divided by the number of items answered on that scale (excluding "Not applicable" and "Prefer not to answer" from both numerator and denominator). Computed only for respondents answering ≥ 11 of the 22 items; otherwise treated as missing.

Perceived prevalence score (primary predictor for H1): mean of band-midpoint values across the same 22 items, excluding "No opinion." Same ≥ 11-item threshold applies.

QRP frequency score (robustness check): mean of ordinal codes (Never=0, Once=1, 2–3 times=2, More than 3 times=3) across valid items, in place of the binary admission rate.

Breadth (descriptive only): count of distinct practices ever admitted (range 0–22).

Open-practices count: count of the 5 open-practice items with any use reported (Once or more).

Publication-pressure composite: mean of the 3 pressure items (institutional/funder pressure, effect on design/reporting, field rewards) on the 1–5 scale, computed only if internal consistency (McDonald's ω) ≥ .60; otherwise these items are analysed individually. The fourth item (perceived detectability) is kept as a standalone variable, not included in this composite.

Career stage (collapsed): recoded from 7 levels into 3 ordered levels for RQ1 - doctoral researcher; postdoctoral/lecturer/assistant professor/senior researcher; associate professor/reader/full professor - with "Outside academia or other" and "Prefer not to answer" excluded from the ordinal test.
table.statistical_tests:
RQ1. Admission rate regressed on career stage (3 collapsed ordered levels) using a linear trend contrast, with Kruskal-Wallis as a distribution-free companion. A second, adjusted model adds publication count, quantitative-work extent, and region as covariates. Both unadjusted and adjusted results are reported. Robustness check: years since PhD substituted for career stage.

RQ2. Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing, across the 22 items, mean perceived prevalence against observed admission proportion (paired at the item level, not the person level).

RQ3. Per-item admission proportion for each of the 22 practices, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals, reported individually. Particular attention to the five music-specific items, for which per-item n will be smaller due to "not applicable" responses and for which no prior estimate exists in any field.

RQ4. Spearman correlation of admission rate with open-practices count, followed by inclusion as one predictor in the multiple regression described under RQ4/H1 below (admission rate regressed on perceived prevalence, publication pressure, detectability, open-practices count, career stage, and publication count).

H1. Linear regression: standardised QRP admission rate regressed on standardised mean perceived prevalence (both computed across the 22 practice items, per-person). H1 is supported if β > 0 with a CI excluding zero. Two-tailed test, α = .05.

H1a. Mixed-effects logistic regression on the 22 items nested within respondents: binary admission (yes/no) predicted by perceived prevalence for that item, decomposed into a between-person mean and a within-person deviation, with random intercepts for respondent and for item.
table.transformations: Practice-item response scales are converted to numeric codes before use: the 4-point frequency scale (Never/Once/2–3 times/More than 3 times) is coded 0–3 for the frequency composite and dichotomised (0 = Never, 1 = anything else) for admission-based measures. "Not applicable to my research" and "Prefer not to answer" are coded as missing, not as 0, and excluded from denominators. The 6-band prevalence-estimate scale is recoded to interval band midpoints, with "No opinion" coded missing. Career stage (7 categorical levels) is collapsed into 3 ordered levels for RQ1 (doctoral; postdoc/lecturer/assistant professor/senior researcher; associate/full professor), with "Outside academia or other" and "Prefer not to answer" excluded from that ordinal test only. QRP admission rate and mean perceived prevalence are standardised (z-scored) before entry into the H1 regression; all other predictors are entered in their natural coding. No other transformation, centering, or recoding is applied.
table.inference_criteria: H1 as the confirmatory test: inference is based on the standardised regression coefficient (β), its 95% confidence interval, and a two-tailed test at α = .05, with support for H1 defined as β > 0 and a CI excluding zero. All other analyses (H1a and RQ1-RQ4) are secondary or exploratory and are reported with effect sizes and confidence intervals instead of accept/reject decisions; p-values there are descriptive, not confirmatory. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied across the secondary/exploratory analyses, on the grounds that adjusting within a family of non-confirmatory tests would misrepresent them as confirmatory. Model convergence (for the mixed-effects model) and assumption checks (linearity, residual normality for the regressions) are treated as prerequisites, not inference criteria: a violation or convergence failure triggers the pre-specified fallback, but does not itself change the inference rule for H1.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Respondents are excluded if they do not consent (Q1 ≠ Yes) or report no empirical authorship in music psychology or an adjacent field in the past five to seven years (Q2 = No). No further exclusion is applied based on methodological approach, research area, or career stage; "Not applicable" response options handle cases where an item does not fit a respondent's work. For inclusion in any person-level composite (admission rate, prevalence score), a respondent must have answered at least 11 of the 22 practice items on the relevant scale; below that, the composite is treated as missing for that respondent, though their answered items still contribute to the per-item descriptive rates (RQ3). No outliers are excluded from any measure, as all variables are bounded ordinal/categorical scales with no continuous distribution to screen for extreme values.
table.missing_data_handling: No imputation method is used given the anonymous, single-wave design and the risk that missingness on questions about QRP use is not missing at random. All models use listwise deletion on the variables entered into that specific model; a respondent missing a required variable is dropped from that analysis but retained in others where their data is complete. "Not applicable" and "Prefer not to answer" are always treated as missing, never recoded as a substantive response (e.g., never as 0 or "Never"), and per-item missingness/refusal rates are reported alongside every proportion.

Publication-pressure composite: mean of the 3 pressure items (institutional/funder pressure, effect on design/reporting, field rewards) on the 1–5 scale, computed only if internal consistency (McDonald's ω) ≥ .60; otherwise these items are analysed individually. The fourth item (perceived detectability) is kept as a standalone variable, not included in this composite.

Career stage (collapsed): recoded from 7 levels into 3 ordered levels for RQ1 - doctoral researcher; postdoctoral/lecturer/assistant professor/senior researcher; associate professor/reader/full professor - with \"Outside academia or other\" and \"Prefer not to answer\" excluded from the ordinal test.", "RQ1. Admission rate regressed on career stage (3 collapsed ordered levels) using a linear trend contrast, with Kruskal-Wallis as a distribution-free companion. A second, adjusted model adds publication count, quantitative-work extent, and region as covariates. Both unadjusted and adjusted results are reported. Robustness check: years since PhD substituted for career stage.

RQ2. Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing, across the 22 items, mean perceived prevalence against observed admission proportion (paired at the item level, not the person level).

RQ3. Per-item admission proportion for each of the 22 practices, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals, reported individually. Particular attention to the five music-specific items, for which per-item n will be smaller due to \"not applicable\" responses and for which no prior estimate exists in any field.

RQ4. Spearman correlation of admission rate with open-practices count, followed by inclusion as one predictor in the multiple regression described under RQ4/H1 below (admission rate regressed on perceived prevalence, publication pressure, detectability, open-practices count, career stage, and publication count).

H1. Linear regression: standardised QRP admission rate regressed on standardised mean perceived prevalence (both computed across the 22 practice items, per-person). H1 is supported if β > 0 with a CI excluding zero. Two-tailed test, α = .05.

H1a. Mixed-effects logistic regression on the 22 items nested within respondents: binary admission (yes/no) predicted by perceived prevalence for that item, decomposed into a between-person mean and a within-person deviation, with random intercepts for respondent and for item.", "Practice-item response scales are converted to numeric codes before use: the 4-point frequency scale (Never/Once/2–3 times/More than 3 times) is coded 0–3 for the frequency composite and dichotomised (0 = Never, 1 = anything else) for admission-based measures. \"Not applicable to my research\" and \"Prefer not to answer\" are coded as missing, not as 0, and excluded from denominators. The 6-band prevalence-estimate scale is recoded to interval band midpoints, with \"No opinion\" coded missing. Career stage (7 categorical levels) is collapsed into 3 ordered levels for RQ1 (doctoral; postdoc/lecturer/assistant professor/senior researcher; associate/full professor), with \"Outside academia or other\" and \"Prefer not to answer\" excluded from that ordinal test only. QRP admission rate and mean perceived prevalence are standardised (z-scored) before entry into the H1 regression; all other predictors are entered in their natural coding. No other transformation, centering, or recoding is applied.", "H1 as the confirmatory test: inference is based on the standardised regression coefficient (β), its 95% confidence interval, and a two-tailed test at α = .05, with support for H1 defined as β > 0 and a CI excluding zero. All other analyses (H1a and RQ1-RQ4) are secondary or exploratory and are reported with effect sizes and confidence intervals instead of accept/reject decisions; p-values there are descriptive, not confirmatory. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied across the secondary/exploratory analyses, on the grounds that adjusting within a family of non-confirmatory tests would misrepresent them as confirmatory. Model convergence (for the mixed-effects model) and assumption checks (linearity, residual normality for the regressions) are treated as prerequisites, not inference criteria: a violation or convergence failure triggers the pre-specified fallback, but does not itself change the inference rule for H1.", "Respondents are excluded if they do not consent (Q1 ≠ Yes) or report no empirical authorship in music psychology or an adjacent field in the past five to seven years (Q2 = No). No further exclusion is applied based on methodological approach, research area, or career stage; \"Not applicable\" response options handle cases where an item does not fit a respondent's work. For inclusion in any person-level composite (admission rate, prevalence score), a respondent must have answered at least 11 of the 22 practice items on the relevant scale; below that, the composite is treated as missing for that respondent, though their answered items still contribute to the per-item descriptive rates (RQ3). No outliers are excluded from any measure, as all variables are bounded ordinal/categorical scales with no continuous distribution to screen for extreme values.", "No imputation method is used given the anonymous, single-wave design and the risk that missingness on questions about QRP use is not missing at random. All models use listwise deletion on the variables entered into that specific model; a respondent missing a required variable is dropped from that analysis but retained in others where their data is complete. \"Not applicable\" and \"Prefer not to answer\" are always treated as missing, never recoded as a substantive response (e.g., never as 0 or \"Never\"), and per-item missingness/refusal rates are reported alongside every proportion.", "input")), row.names = c("template_name", "title", "id", "link", "date_created", "date_modified", "date_registered", "embargo_end_date", "ia_url", "research_questions", "foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence", "study_type", "intention_for_causal_interpretation", "blinding", "study_design_overview", "data_collection_procedures", "sample_size", "sample_size_rationale", "stopping_rule", "manipulated_variables", "measured_variables", "indices", "statistical_tests", "transformations", "inference_criteria", "data_exclusion_criteria", "missing_data_handling", "paper_id"), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of deviations from preregistrations, see: van den Akker O, Bakker M, van Assen M, Pennington C, Verweij L, Elsherif M, Claesen A, Gaillard S, Yeung S, Frankenberger J, Krautter K, Cockcroft J, Kreuer K, Evans T, Heppel F, Schoch S, Korbmacher M, Yamada Y, Albayrak-Aydemir N, Wicherts J (2024). “The potential of preregistration in psychology: Assessing preregistration producibility and preregistration-study consistency.” Psychological Methods. doi:10.1037/met0000687. #### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. #### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: (Anthropic) to assist with debugging the R code for the analyses, tables and figures.
The authors reviewed, ran and verified all code and output, checked the results against the data, and take full responsibility for the content of the manuscript.
Overt scientific misconduct attracts the headlines.
Fabrication and falsification make for compelling narratives of individual wrongdoing, and high-profile cases have kept research integrity in public view (Thorp, 2023).
text.formatted: Fabrication and falsification make for compelling narratives of individual wrongdoing, and high-profile cases have kept research integrity in public view <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Thorp, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Questionable research practices (QRPs) may likely be a larger problem.

National surveys indicate that roughly 40% to 51% of researchers admit to at least one such practice (for the Netherlands, see Gopalakrishna et al., 2022;  for Norway, see Kaiser et al., 2022; and Denmark, UK, US, Croatia and Austria, see Schneider et al., 2024), and the practices themselves occupy an ambiguous territory between defensible methodological flexibility and decisions that compromise inference (Nagy et al., 2025; Ravn & Sørensen, 2021).
text.formatted: National surveys indicate that roughly 40% to 51% of researchers admit to at least one such practice (for the Netherlands, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Gopalakrishna et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for Norway, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kaiser et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">and</ref> Denmark, UK, US, Croatia and Austria, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Schneider et al., 2024)</ref>, and the practices themselves occupy an ambiguous territory between defensible methodological flexibility and decisions that compromise inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Nagy et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ravn & Sørensen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The consequences are not ambiguous.

Excluding observations after inspecting the data, selectively reporting outcomes or revising an analytical strategy once the results are known can raise the probability of a statistically significant finding when the hypothesis is false (Simmons et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Excluding observations after inspecting the data, selectively reporting outcomes or revising an analytical strategy once the results are known can raise the probability of a statistically significant finding when the hypothesis is false <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Simmons et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Simulation studies (i.e., studies that test these practices on artificial data where the true answer is known; Stefan & Schönbrodt, 2023) show that p-hacking can substantially inflate false-positive rates above the nominal 5% level (Stefan & Schönbrodt, 2023).
text.formatted: Simulation studies (i.e., studies that test these practices on artificial data where the true answer is known; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stefan & Schönbrodt, 2023)</ref> show that p-hacking can substantially inflate false-positive rates above the nominal 5% level <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Stefan & Schönbrodt, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, Kravitz and Mitroff (2023) found that reusing pilot data and collecting additional observations after checking for significance increased false discoveries in data generated under a true null hypothesis.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Kravitz and Mitroff (2023)</ref> found that reusing pilot data and collecting additional observations after checking for significance increased false discoveries in data generated under a true null hypothesis.

text.text: Estimates of the resulting damage are more modest.

One analysis of psychology articles put the share of false positives among significant results at around 18% (Schneck, 2023), and whether QRPs fully account for replication failure remains contested (Rubin, 2024).
text.formatted: One analysis of psychology articles put the share of false positives among significant results at around 18% <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Schneck, 2023)</ref>, and whether QRPs fully account for replication failure remains contested <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Rubin, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The concern, then, is not confined to deliberate deception.
Ordinary analytical decisions, insufficiently justified or undisclosed, can distort a claim's evidential basis.
Understanding QRPs therefore requires attention to the environments in which those decisions are taken.

Researchers form expectations about acceptable methods, reporting conventions, and peers' conduct, and those expectations vary by field: a practice treated as questionable in one area is considered good practice in another (Ravn & Sørensen, 2021).
text.formatted: Researchers form expectations about acceptable methods, reporting conventions, and peers' conduct, and those expectations vary by field: a practice treated as questionable in one area is considered good practice in another <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ravn & Sørensen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptions of the research climate account for considerably more variance in perceived misbehaviour than individual characteristics do (Haven et al., 2021), and subscription to counternorms has been associated with 40% to 60% of QRP prevalence in a large cross-field survey (Karabağ et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Perceptions of the research climate account for considerably more variance in perceived misbehaviour than individual characteristics do <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Haven et al., 2021)</ref>, and subscription to counternorms has been associated with 40% to 60% of QRP prevalence in a large cross-field survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Karabağ et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Two reasons warrant caution:
First, beliefs about what colleagues do are not the same as beliefs about what colleagues approve of, a distinction drawn sharply in the wider norms literature (Gavrilets et al., 2024).
text.formatted: First, beliefs about what colleagues do are not the same as beliefs about what colleagues approve of, a distinction drawn sharply in the wider norms literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gavrilets et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Second, researchers appear to know little about what their peers actually do: in quantitative criminology, estimates of others' prevalence approximated a uniform distribution (Chin et al., 2023), and perceived seriousness correlates negatively with admitted frequency (Entradas et al., 2026; Larsson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Second, researchers appear to know little about what their peers actually do: in quantitative criminology, estimates of others' prevalence approximated a uniform distribution <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chin et al., 2023)</ref>, and perceived seriousness correlates negatively with admitted frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Entradas et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Larsson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Perceived prevalence offers insight into the social context of research but does not provide an accurate estimate of behaviour.
Institutional conditions influence the opportunities and incentives attached to these practices.

Publication pressure is among the strongest single predictors of self-reported misconduct (Maggio et al., 2019), accounting for 19% of the variance in one disciplinary survey (Heuritsch, 2021), and the broader architecture of output-based reward has been identified as the mechanism sustaining QRPs in exercise and health science specifically (Tiller & Ekkekakis, 2023).
text.formatted: Publication pressure is among the strongest single predictors of self-reported misconduct <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Maggio et al., 2019)</ref>, accounting for 19% of the variance in one disciplinary survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Heuritsch, 2021)</ref>, and the broader architecture of output-based reward has been identified as the mechanism sustaining QRPs in exercise and health science specifically <ref type="bibr">(Tiller & Ekkekakis, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Career stage may also matter, although findings are mixed.

Junior researchers report more frequent QRPs and fewer responsible research practices (Brooker & Allum, 2024; Gopalakrishna et al., 2022), and face greater barriers to open research, including limited time and training, fear of scrutiny, and peer resistance (Alter et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Junior researchers report more frequent QRPs and fewer responsible research practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brooker & Allum, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Gopalakrishna et al., 2022)</ref>, and face greater barriers to open research, including limited time and training, fear of scrutiny, and peer resistance <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alter et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, Fraser et al. (2018) found no consistent association between seniority and QRP use in ecology and evolution.
text.formatted: However, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Fraser et al. (2018)</ref> found no consistent association between seniority and QRP use in ecology and evolution.

text.text: QRPs also vary across the research lifecycle: analytical and reporting decisions are distinct from practices involving stimuli, publishing, and citation, particularly in their rationale and reliance on disclosure (Ravn & Sørensen, 2021).
text.formatted: QRPs also vary across the research lifecycle: analytical and reporting decisions are distinct from practices involving stimuli, publishing, and citation, particularly in their rationale and reliance on disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ravn & Sørensen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, open research practices are not simply the inverse of QRP engagement.

Although support for open practices and support for QRPs are inversely related (Chin et al., 2023), communication researchers reported using QRPs while rejecting them and overestimating their prevalence among peers, alongside positive attitudes towards open research practices (Bakker et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Although support for open practices and support for QRPs are inversely related <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chin et al., 2023)</ref>, communication researchers reported using QRPs while rejecting them and overestimating their prevalence among peers, alongside positive attitudes towards open research practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bakker et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Adopting open research practices does not guarantee that research decisions were appropriate or that researchers documented deviations from preregistered plans (Poole et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Adopting open research practices does not guarantee that research decisions were appropriate or that researchers documented deviations from preregistered plans <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Poole et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Investigating QRPs thus requires distinguishing self-reported behaviour from perceived colleague behaviour, while considering their associations with career stage and engagement with open research practices.
This is particularly important in fields where direct evidence remains limited.
In music psychology, a publication audit from 2017 to 2022 found that only 5% shared raw data, 1% shared analysis scripts, and none reported preregistration (Eerola, 2025).
text.formatted: In music psychology, a publication audit from 2017 to 2022 found that only 5% shared raw data, 1% shared analysis scripts, and none reported preregistration <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Eerola, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, the prevalence of QRPs in the field remains unknown.

The present study provides a first estimate of self-reported QRPs in music psychology and examines how they relate to perceived colleague behaviour, career stage and engagement with open research practices.
We examined whether perceived colleague use was associated with personal admissions, separating variation across respondents from variation across practices within respondents (H1 and H1a).

Four questions followed: whether self-reported engagement varied with career stage (RQ1); whether perceived colleague use exceeded self-reported use (RQ2); whether engagement differed across music-specific, reporting and analysis, and publishing and citation practices (RQ3); and whether engagement with open research practices was associated with QRP admissions (RQ4).
we found eight ineligible (all stated that they had not authored empirical research in the past five to seven years, and none answered any practice questions), leaving 199 eligible respondents.
We excluded no eligible respondents from the primary analyses.
We found no identical response patterns among eligible respondents, although anonymity and the absence of IP-address recording prevent us from ruling out repeated submissions.
As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the personlevel models after excluding respondents who gave identical answers to all prevalence questions (n = 9 of 154).

The sample comprised 18 doctoral researchers, 39 postdoctoral researchers, 45 lecturers or senior researchers, 33 associate professors, 52 full professors, and eight respondents working outside academia; four did not report their career stage.
Among respondents reporting their stage, 26.7% were full professors.
Most respondents were based in Europe (61.2%).

Participation was voluntary, and questions were optional except for consent and eligibility.
No direct identifiers were collected, IP addresses were not recorded, and invitation records were not linked to survey responses.
Participants received a research notification and GDPR-compliant privacy notice, provided electronic informed consent, and were informed of their data-protection rights.
The study was assessed against [withheld for blind review] criteria for ethical review; none applied to this anonymous questionnaire of consenting adult researchers.
The research notification and privacy notice are provided as supplementary materials (S4, S5).
The questionnaire adapted research-practice items from John et al. (2012) and Fraser et al. (2018), with publishing and citation practices informed by Schneider et al. (2024).

text.text: Five additional items addressed music-specific practices.
The 22 items covered reporting and analysis (Items 1-13), music-specific practices (Items 14-18), and publishing and citation (Items 19-22).

Examples included omitting outcomes or conditions, optional stopping, selecting analyses after inspecting results, presenting exploratory findings as prespecified, changing musical stimuli after observing results, selecting audio features or preprocessing pipelines, undisclosed data reuse, and selective citation.
Full item wording is provided in Appendix A (Tables A1 and A2).

text.text: Item 12 concerned deviations from preregistration and therefore applied only to researchers who preregistered.
Differences in wording, including whether items explicitly specified that a practice was undertaken without reporting it, may influence comparisons between items and blocks.
Although a separate "not applicable" response was available, some respondents may have interpreted "Never" as meaning the practice was inapplicable to their research.
Respondents reported how often they had engaged in each practice during the past five to seven years, using four frequency categories: Never, Once, 2-3 times, and More than 3 times.
Respondents could answer "Not applicable to my research" and "Prefer not to answer"; both were treated as missing.
"Not applicable" was chosen for 431 of the 4,378 own use answers (9.8%; 106 respondents, most often for items 12, 17 and 18), "prefer not to answer" for 32 (0.7%) and 47 (1.1%) were left blank.
Following Fiedler and Schwarz (2016), we examined both own use (reporting a practice at least once) and the reported frequency distribution.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Fiedler and Schwarz (2016)</ref>, we examined both own use (reporting a practice at least once) and the reported frequency distribution.

text.text: After completing the own-use items, respondents estimated the percentage of musicpsychology researchers who had engaged in each practice at least once during the same period.
They chose one of five ranges (0-10%, 11-25%, 26-50%, 51-75% or 76-100%) or "no opinion".
We scored each estimate at the mid point of its range (5%, 18%, 38%, 63%, and 88%, respectively).
"No opinion" was chosen for 904 of 4,378 estimates (20.6%) and treated as missing.
Respondents reported the frequency of five open-science practices: preregistration, data sharing, code or materials sharing, attempted replication, and preprint posting.

They also rated four statements concerning publication pressure on five-point agreement scales and provided demographic and professional information, including career stage, years since PhD, region, gender, research area, publication count, and typical sample size.
Analyses were conducted in R 4.6.1.
We fitted mixed-effects models using lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and processed data with dplyr (Wickham et al., 2023).
text.formatted: We fitted mixed-effects models using lme4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref> and processed data with dplyr <ref type="bibr">(Wickham et al., 2023)</ref>.

H1 and H1a were confirmatory; all other analyses were exploratory.
Analyses not preregistered are identified in Table S3.

text.text: For each practice, we calculated the proportion of respondents reporting at least one engagement, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (the continuity correction was omitted as it makes intervals slightly conservative; across the 22 items it changed the interval limits by at most 0.5 percentage points), and the mean perceived prevalence, scored using the midpoints of the response categories.
We summarised each research practice category in two ways: the proportion of respondents reporting at least one practice in the category and the mean item-level prevalence of self-reported use.
We calculated overall rates both for Items 1-18 and for all 22 items, distinguishing practices potentially associated with inflated false-positive rates from publishing and citation practices.
For H1, H1a, and RQ1, we calculated each respondent's admission rate as the proportion of valid own-use responses indicating engagement in a practice at least once.
Inclusion required at least 11 valid own-use responses out of 22; H1 additionally required at least 11 valid perceivedprevalence estimates.
These criteria excluded 14 respondents for insufficient own-use data and 37 for insufficient prevalence data; six failed both criteria.
The resulting sample for the H1 models comprised 154 respondents.
H1 was tested using a quasi-binomial model predicting the number of practices admitted out of the number answered, with standardised mean perceived prevalence as the predictor.
H1a was tested using a logistic mixed-effects model with random intercepts for respondents and items.
The predictors were respondents' mean perceived-prevalence estimates (between-person differences) and deviations from each respondent's mean (within-person differences).
We standardised both, so the corresponding odds ratios represent changes per standard deviation.

As own use and perceived prevalence were strongly correlated across items (r = .87), the within-person association may partly indicate item-level differences instead of an independent respondent-level process.
We therefore fitted additional models centring estimates on both respondent and item means and including a respondent-level random slope.
RQ1 concerned differences in admission rates across career stages.
We examined these differences using an F test from a quasi-binomial model and a Kruskal-Wallis test.
We also estimated the Spearman correlation between career stage and admission rate, with a bootstrap interval, and calculated mean admission rates for each career stage.
These complementary analyses allowed us to examine both differences between career-stage groups and the association across the ordered stages.
To address RQ2, we calculated the difference between mean perceived prevalence and observed own use for each item.

As perceived prevalence was assessed using five bounded response categories, these differences cannot be interpreted without considering the tendency of categorical estimates to regress towards the centre of the scale.

We therefore regressed mean perceived prevalence on observed own use, using both percentage and logit scales, to establish a descriptive reference against which we could examine item-level discrepancies.
We also calculated the proportion of respondents whose estimates fell above or below the response category containing the observed rate.
We quantified uncertainty in the observed rates, mean estimates, and deviations from the regression reference using 5,000 respondent-level bootstrap samples.
We calculated Bonferroni-adjusted simultaneous intervals for the 22 item-level deviations.
The regression reference is not a null model: it may also absorb substantive patterns, including greater underreporting of less prevalent or more socially undesirable practices.
We therefore interpreted the sign test across items alongside the regression results.

For RQ3, we compared self-reported own use across the three research practice categories using a logistic mixed-effects model, with the research practice category as a fixed effect and random intercepts for respondents and items.
These comparisons require caution as the applicability of some practices differs across researchers, and the response "Never" may not always indicate that a practice was applicable but unused.

We therefore conducted exploratory sensitivity analyses restricting Item 12 to respondents who had preregistered, Items 14-16 to respondents reporting a typical sample size, and Items 17-18 to research areas in which the relevant audio, physiological, or neural methods were plausible.

We also estimated how many "Never" responses in the musicspecific research practice category would need to indicate inapplicability for its prevalence to equal that of the comparison research practice categories.

As item wording differed in whether it explicitly qualified a practice as undertaken without reporting it, we further compared items with and without this qualifier separately and included the qualifier as a fixed effect.
These restrictions are approximate indicators of applicability, and the research practice category comparisons outside the descriptive analyses were exploratory.
For RQ4, we examined whether engagement in open-science practices was associated with admission rates.
A quasi-binomial model related the number of open-science practices reported (0-5) to the proportion of admitted practices.
As Item 12 concerned deviations from preregistration, its applicability was structurally linked to one of the predictors.
We therefore refitted the model excluding Item 12 and, separately, using only the four other open-science practices.

We also adjusted for career stage, publication count, and typical sample size to account for differences in research experience and opportunities to engage in both open-science and questionable research practices.
Adding the same covariates to the H1 and H1a models did not materially change the results (odds ratios changed by 0.03 or less).

In addition, we adjusted for agreement that reviewers or collaborators would detect questionable practices as a rough indicator of awareness, and included the open-science predictor in the crossed mixed-effects model used for H1a.
Finally, we repeated the analysis using the summed frequency scores of the five open-science practices (0-15), instead of their count.

As a final sensitivity analysis, we compared the main findings between all eligible respondents and those who identified a music-research area, excluding respondents who selected "Other" or "Prefer not to answer".

Of 193 respondents with at least one valid answer to Items 1-18, 145 (75.1%, 95% CI [68.6, 80.7]) reported having engaged in at least one practice potentially associated with inflated false-positive rates.
Among the 198 respondents with valid answers to the full set, 164 (82.8%, 95% CI [77.0, 87.4]) reported at least one of the 22 practices.
Respondents reported a mean of 2.82 practices among Items 1-18 and 3.55 across all 22 items.
Prevalence varied substantially across individual practices (Table 1; Figure 1).
text.formatted: Prevalence varied substantially across individual practices (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The most frequently reported practices were citing irrelevant work to please a reviewer (46.9%, 95% CI [40.0, 53.9]), selecting the most favourable analysis (43.5%, [36.5, 50.7]), and reporting a p-value above the conventional threshold as statistically or marginally significant (30.0%, [23.8, 37.1]).
The least frequently reported were undisclosed reuse of data (4.2%, [2.1, 8.0]) and changing stimuli after observing the results (5.3%, [2.8, 9.8]).
Admissions were not limited to isolated occurrences.
Of all responses indicating own use, 47.7% were classified as "Once", 42.0% as "2-3 times", and 10.3% as "More than 3 times".
Thus, 52.3% of admissions indicated repeated use during the reference period.
Respondents who perceived QRPs to be more prevalent reported engaging in more of them.

In the quasi-binomial model testing H1, each standard-deviation increase in mean perceived prevalence was associated with 1.81 times the odds of admitting a practice (95% CI [1.58, 2.08], p < .001, n = 154; Spearman's ρ = .57).

Bootstrap confidence intervals excluded zero on the positive side for 12 practices and on the negative side for two: selecting the most favourable analysis and citing irrelevant work to please a reviewer (Table 1; Figure 1).

text.text: The magnitude of the discrepancy depended strongly on observed prevalence.
Across the 22 practices, the difference between perceived and observed prevalence correlated negatively with observed use (r = -.89).
Mean perceived prevalence increased by 0.48 percentage points for each percentage-point increase in observed use (95% bootstrap CI [0.40, 0.54]; intercept = 15.8; R² = .75).
The corresponding logit-scale slope was 0.37.
The fitted regression crossed the line of equality at approximately 30.2% observed use (Figure 2).
text.formatted: The fitted regression crossed the line of equality at approximately 30.2% observed use (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: This pattern indicates substantial compression of prevalence estimates towards the middle of the response scale.
Practices reported by relatively few respondents were generally estimated at 16-20% prevalence, whereas the most frequently reported practices tended to be underestimated.
The scoring procedure contributed to this pattern: the lowest response category was assigned a value of 5%, already exceeding the observed prevalence of undisclosed data reuse (4.2%).
Conversely, the observed prevalence of selecting the most favourable analysis and citing irrelevant work exceeded the corresponding mean estimates.
Nine practices had residuals whose bootstrap confidence intervals excluded zero relative to the regression reference.

Perceived prevalence was higher than the reference for salami slicing (+9.1 percentage points), shelving non-significant studies (+5.0), presenting exploratory analyses as confirmatory (+3.4), HARKing (+2.6), and omitting contradictory findings (+2.5).

It was lower for applying post hoc musical-background criteria (-5.0), omitting experimental conditions (-4.3), failing to report deviations from preregistration (-2.8), and changing stimuli after observing results (-2.1).

After Bonferroni adjustment, four residuals remained distinguishable from zero: salami slicing and shelving non-significant studies were above the reference, whereas omitting conditions and applying post hoc musical-background criteria were below it.
These deviations are relative to a descriptive regression reference (i.e., not evidence of absolute overestimation or underestimation).
The five music-specific practices were reported by 5.3-17.2% of respondents (Table 1).
text.formatted: The five music-specific practices were reported by 5.3-17.2% of respondents (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Changing stimuli after observing results (5.3%) and defining musical training after observing results (6.0%) were among the least frequently reported practices overall.

Applying post hoc musical-background criteria was reported by 13.0% of respondents, selecting audio or music-information-retrieval features post hoc by 7.7%, and selecting preprocessing pipelines post hoc by 17.2%.
None ranked among the three most frequently reported practices.
Valid response counts were lower for these items (n = 128-177) than for most other items (suggestive that some practices were inapplicable to respondents' research).

In the crossed logistic mixed-effects model, the odds of reporting a musicspecific practice were lower than those of reporting a reporting and analysis practice (OR = 0.35, 95% CI [0.14, 0.89], p = .027; Figure 3).

text.text: The estimate was similar when the analysis was restricted to respondents with at least three valid music-specific answers (OR = 0.35, [0.14, 0.84], p = .019).
Publishing and citation practices did not differ detectably from reporting and analysis practices (OR = 0.83, [0.31, 2.20], p = .702; Table 2).

text.text: The music-specific contrast remained similar when Item 12 was restricted to respondents who had preregistered and when Items 14-18 were restricted to respondents for whom the relevant practices were considered plausibly applicable (OR = 0.34 and 0.37, respectively).
Under the strictest restriction, the pooled music-specific admission rate was 10.1%, compared with 20.8% for reporting and analysis practices.
For these rates to be equal, an estimated 54.0% of valid music-specific responses, or 59.7% of "Never" responses, would have to reflect inapplicability.
However, the applicability restrictions are only approximate and cannot determine how many "Never" responses represented genuinely irrelevant practices.
Item wording also influenced the comparison.

Among items without an explicit "without reporting this" qualifier, the odds of reporting music-specific practices were lower than those of reporting general practices (OR = 0.29, 95% CI [0.10, 0.84], p = .023).
Among qualified items, the difference was not detectable (OR = 0.82, [0.39, 1.73], p = .596).
Including the qualifier as a fixed effect yielded an overall music-specific contrast of OR = 0.43 ([0.19, 0.97], p = .042).
As only two general items carried the qualifier, this comparison was limited.
The lower reported prevalence of music-specific practices was therefore broadly robust to the applicability checks, but its magnitude depended on item wording.

text.text: These findings indicate a positive association between open-science engagement and self-reported QRP use in this sample.
The main findings were similar when analyses were restricted to the 159 respondents who identified a music-research area.
In this subsample, 76.1% reported at least one of Items 1-18, the H1 odds ratio was 1.93 (95% CI [1.65, 2.24]), and the RQ4 odds ratio was 1.27 ([1.12, 1.45]).

Admission rates varied across response phases.

All 17 eligible respondents who completed the survey before the first personal mailing reported at least one of Items 1-18, compared with 71.6% of those responding between the first mailing and the reminder and 75.0% of those responding after the reminder.

The early respondents also had a higher mean admission rate (24.0%) than the remainder of the sample (17.4%; Wilcoxon p = .020; Fisher's exact test, p = .008), although this comparison involved a small group.

By contrast, respondents who completed the survey after the reminder did not differ detectably from earlier respondents in the proportion reporting at least one practice (75.0% vs 75.2%, Fisher's exact p = 1.000) or mean admission rate (17.0% vs 18.5%, Wilcoxon p = .695).
Admission rate was not associated with response timing across the field period (ρ = -.06, p = .383).

Most respondents agreed that their institution or funders pressured them to publish frequently (57.6%) and that researchers in the field were rewarded more for publishing quantity than for conducting careful research (56.3%).
Fewer reported that publication pressure had affected how they designed or reported studies (30.3%).
Overall, 41.4% believed that QRPs would be detected by reviewers or collaborators.

This study investigated self-reported QRPs in music psychology and their associations with researchers' perceptions of colleagues' behaviour, career stage, and engagement with open research practices.
H1 was supported: respondents who perceived QRPs to be more prevalent among colleagues also reported greater personal engagement in these practices.
H1a was also supported, with positive associations at both the between-person and within-person levels.
Thus, the association between perceived and self-reported QRP engagement was evident both across respondents and across practices within respondents.
Regarding the research questions, RQ1 yielded no detectable association between career stage and self-reported QRP engagement.

For RQ2, respondents estimated that colleagues engaged in QRPs more frequently than they themselves reported doing for 20 of the 22 practices, although the discrepancy varied across practices and was constrained by the prevalence response scale.

For RQ3, music-specific practices were reported less frequently than reporting and analysis practices in the primary model, whereas publishing and citation practices did not differ detectably from reporting and analysis practices; sensitivity analyses qualified the finding for music-specific practices.
Finally, for RQ4, greater engagement with open research practices was associated with more QRP admissions.
These findings extend survey research on QRPs to music psychology while raising questions about how to interpret personal admissions, perceived norms, and open-science engagement.
Overall, 75.1% of respondents reported having engaged in at least one of the 18 reporting, analysis, and music-specific practices, increasing to 82.8% when all 22 practices were considered.
These proportions are broadly consistent with surveys in other disciplines documenting self-reported QRP engagement (John et al., 2012; Fraser et al., 2018; Gopalakrishna et al., 2022).

text.text: Although this may suggest greater willingness to attribute questionable behaviour to others, both measures are self-reports rather than independent measures of actual behaviour.
The discrepancy could reflect reluctance to disclose personal practices, inaccurate perceptions of colleagues, or both.
Two practices reversed the pattern.
Participants admitted selecting a favourable analysis and citing irrelevant work more often than they attributed these practices to colleagues.
This does not mean either practice is approved of.

Beliefs about what colleagues do are distinct from beliefs about what they approve of, a distinction drawn clearly in the wider norms literature (Gavrilets et al., 2024) and operationalised by John et al. (2012) through defensibility ratings and by Fraser et al. (2018) through should-use items.
We measured neither, so we cannot say whether these reversals indicate perceived acceptability (or something else).
The scale itself limits what the gap can mean.
Assigning 5% to the lowest category already exceeded the observed prevalence of undisclosed data reuse, and estimates compressed towards the middle of the range.
Apparent overestimation of rare practices is therefore partly an artefact of measurement.
Despite this measurement limitation, perceived prevalence remained positively associated with personal admissions at both levels.
This pattern is consistent with a descriptivenorm account, although it does not establish that perceived norms shape behaviour.
Chin et al. (2023) reported similarly uninformative estimates of peer behaviour in criminology, suggesting that researchers' perceptions may poorly indicate what their colleagues actually do.
We found no detectable association between career stage and admissions.

This is consistent with Fraser et al. (2018), who likewise found little evidence of a career gradient, and sits against national surveys reporting more frequent QRPs among junior and insecurely contracted researchers (Brooker & Allum, 2024; Gopalakrishna et al., 2022; Entradas et al., 2026).

text.text: However, sampling, how career experience is operationalised and which outcome is measured all differ across these studies.
With 18 doctoral researchers and seven respondents outside academia, our null result is weakly informative and should not be read as evidence of equivalence.
The lower rate for music-specific practices needs similar care.
The contrast held under applicability restrictions, but it was concentrated among items lacking an explicit 'without reporting this' qualifier.
Wording appears to influence whether a decision registers as questionable at all.
Opportunity matters too, since practices tied to musical stimuli or audio features are simply irrelevant to some respondents, as the lower valid-response counts suggest.
For the categories to be equal, roughly 54% of valid music-specific responses would have to represent inapplicability, which is possible but unverifiable here.
These results do not show that music-specific decisions are less prone to questionable use; they better indicate how hard it is to compare practice categories built from different items.

Over half of respondents perceived pressure to publish frequently (57.6%) or thought the field rewards quantity over care (56.3%), while fewer said this had altered how they designed or reported studies (30.3%).

These perceptions are consistent with accounts locating QRPs partly in institutional incentives (Gopalakrishna et al., 2022; Heuritsch, 2021; Tiller & Ekkekakis, 2023), but they are perceptions, and we cannot show that pressure produced the practices reported here.

text.text: The clearest surprise is that engagement with open research practices was associated with more admissions, and the association survived adjustment for career stage, publication count, and sample size.

This runs against the expectation implicit in much open-science advocacy and against the inverse relationship Chin et al. (2023) found between support for QRPs and support for open practices, though support and behaviour are different things.
text.formatted: This runs against the expectation implicit in much open-science advocacy and against the inverse relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Chin et al. (2023)</ref> found between support for QRPs and support for open practices, though support and behaviour are different things.

text.text: It may be a mistake to read this as evidence that open practices encourage questionable behaviour.

We measured self-reported admissions, not research quality, reproducibility or transparency, and our open-practice measure captured whether someone had ever preregistered or shared data, not whether doing so constrained any particular decision.

Eerola (in press) found that music psychology authors ranked mandates and minimal effort as the conditions most likely to produce data sharing, while recognition and financial reward ranked near the bottom, and they endorsed sharing considerably more for the field than for their own current project.
If researchers adopt open practices mainly as they are required or easy (e.g., a journal policy), then preregistering or sharing data says little about how carefully they make analytic decisions.
The positive association is then less surprising, since the two measures may capture different things.

Other explanations remain: researchers engaged with open science may recognise questionable decisions more readily, having thought harder about methodology; they may be more willing to disclose them; or they may differ in research activity in ways that create more opportunities to encounter the practices we listed.

Adjusting for whether respondents believed reviewers would detect QRPs did not change the estimate, and that belief was unrelated to openpractice engagement, which weakens the simplest detection-based account without settling the question.
The underlying point is that transparency and QRP admission are not two ends of one continuum.

Open practices can make decisions more visible while also sharpening awareness of how those decisions might be classified, and preregistration in particular guarantees neither that the decisions taken were appropriate nor that departures were documented (Poole et al., 2025).

Distinguishing behaviour from its recognition and its disclosure will require designs that do not rely on asking researchers about both.
Participation was voluntary, recruitment combined personal invitations with an open survey link, and the response rate to personal invitations was lower than the 15% reported by Fraser et al. (2018).

text.text: Non-response bias therefore remains a concern.

The available checks provide only limited reassurance: restricting the analysis to respondents who identified a music-research area left the main estimates unchanged, and late respondents did not differ detectably from earlier respondents.

However, late respondents cannot be assumed to represent those who did not participate, and the analysed export did not retain the recruitment route, precluding direct comparisons between recruitment groups.
Self-selection may also have favoured researchers already engaged with methodological debates.

The comparatively high levels of open-practice engagement observed here, relative to previous surveys and audits of music psychology (Eerola, 2025 (Eerola, , 2026)), are consistent with this possibility, although they do not establish it.

text.text: Such selection could restrict the range of open-science engagement in the sample and, in turn, influence the interpretation and generalisability of its association with QRP admissions.
All measures were self-reported and thus susceptible to recall, interpretation, and disclosure biases, including estimates of colleagues' behaviour.
The bounded prevalence scale limited the resolution of estimates for rare practices, while differences in item wording and applicability complicated comparisons across practice categories.
Finally, the cross-sectional design precludes causal conclusions about the relationships among perceived norms, personal admissions, career stage, and engagement with open research practices.
Most respondents reported having engaged in at least one of the practices surveyed, although admissions varied considerably across practices.
Perceived colleague use generally exceeded personal admissions, and the two were positively associated.
However, the low response rate and sensitivity of the behaviours surveyed mean that reported rates may underestimate actual use across the field.
Career stage showed no detectable association with QRP admissions, while differences between practice categories were sensitive to measurement choices.
